beats.text: On its specification sheet, a modern data-centre G P U can perform close to a thousand trillion operations every single second.
Nine hundred and eighty-nine trillion additions and multiplications, packed onto a square of silicon no larger than a postage stamp.
Yet when you ask a language model to generate an answer, that vast engine of arithmetic spends more than ninety-nine percent of its time waiting.

chapter.title: Cold open: a thousand trillion, waiting

beats.text: The arithmetic for one token takes about a tenth of a millisecond. The rest is spent waiting for numbers to arrive from memory.
Between the memory stacks and the chip sits a bus of five thousand one hundred and twenty tiny wires. And those wires set the pace.
Every weight the model uses must cross that bridge, token after token. The chip is not slow; it is starved for data.

chapter.title: Cold open: a thousand trillion, waiting

beats.text: To understand why this happens, we have to look inside the package, down to the transistors and the clock cycles.
Why does fetching one number from memory take five hundred ticks of the clock, while adding two numbers takes only one?
How do sixty-four warps of threads hide that wait, and why does a single wrong turn cut throughput in half?
This is the machine behind the memory wall.
Inside the G P U.

chapter.title: Cold open: a thousand trillion, waiting

beats.text: Here is what you actually hold in your hand: a heavy metal package containing a square of polished silicon, surrounded by memory.
That central square is the compute die, roughly twenty-nine millimetres on a side. It is printed with about eighty billion transistors.
That works out at roughly a hundred million switches packed into every single square millimetre.
Nothing is assembled by hand. The entire pattern is printed with light, all at once, the way a photograph is exposed.
This square is the chip's silicon budget. Every multiprocessor, every cache, and every wire is a slice of this one surface.
Underneath the complexity, a chip is simply a slab of silicon covered in tiny switches.
A transistor lets electrical current through, or blocks it, depending on a control voltage. It is a tap with no in-between position.
Wire a handful of them together, and you have a circuit that adds two binary numbers.
Wire eighty billion of them together, and you have a modern G P U. Everything in this machine is made of nothing but these.
To understand how those switches do work, we need three words: an instruction, a cycle, and a thread.
An instruction is one single thing the chip is told to do: add two numbers, fetch a value from memory, or jump somewhere else.
A clock cycle is one tick of the chip's internal clock. A modern chip ticks well over a billion times a second.
That means one cycle lasts about half a nanosecond, a billionth of a second. A cycle is the unit of time at this scale.
A thread is simply a sequence of instructions being executed one after another. A chip running many threads handles many sequences at the same time.

chapter.title: Two numbers and the words around them
chapter.kicker: 02 · Two numbers and the words around them

beats.text: Two numbers on the specification sheet predict almost everything about inference speed: arithmetic rate, and memory bandwidth.
Yet performance claims constantly confuse count with rate, and latency with bandwidth. We need to keep them apart.
A flop is one single operation, a count with no time in it. Flops per second is a rate.
Divide the count of operations by the rate, and you get seconds. A hundred and forty billion operations at nine hundred and eighty-nine trillion a second takes zero point one four milliseconds.
Latency is how long one request takes to return. Bandwidth is how many bytes arrive per second when many requests travel together.

chapter.title: Two numbers and the words around them
chapter.kicker: 02 · Two numbers and the words around them

beats.text: Whenever a specification quotes operations per second or bytes per second, it is quoting throughput.
Throughput counts what leaves the machine every second. It says nothing about how long any single item spent inside.
That is the exact trade a G P U makes. It runs each thread slowly, but runs an enormous number of them, so the volume leaving per second is huge.

chapter.title: Two numbers and the words around them
chapter.kicker: 02 · Two numbers and the words around them

beats.text: A bus is simply a bundle of wires joining memory to the chip. Its bandwidth equals the number of wires, times how fast each wire runs.
Compare two real chips. A high-end gaming card, the R T X forty ninety, has three hundred and eighty-four wires running at twenty-one billion bits a second each.
The H one hundred runs its wires four times slower, at only five point two four billion bits a second.
Yet the H one hundred moves more than three times as many bytes every second, because it has over thirteen times as many wires.

chapter.title: Two numbers and the words around them
chapter.kicker: 02 · Two numbers and the words around them

beats.text: On the H one hundred, five stacks of high-bandwidth memory are placed directly beside the compute die.
Each stack connects through one thousand and twenty-four data wires. Five stacks give five thousand one hundred and twenty wires in all.
Each wire ticks two thousand six hundred and nineteen million times a second, transferring one bit on the rise and one on the fall.
Multiply by five thousand wires, divide by eight bits per byte, and you arrive at three thousand three hundred and fifty-two gigabytes per second: the three point three five terabytes on the box.

chapter.title: Two numbers and the words around them
chapter.kicker: 02 · Two numbers and the words around them

beats.text: To picture how time unfolds inside the machine, we need a logarithmic scale, where each equal step is ten times longer.
At the left sits one clock tick: about zero point five five nanoseconds.
A single load from memory takes about two hundred and seventy nanoseconds. That is nearly five hundred clock ticks.
At the far right sits one generated token: about thirty milliseconds, or more than a hundred thousand memory loads.

chapter.title: Two numbers and the words around them
chapter.kicker: 02 · Two numbers and the words around them

beats.text: Take one decode step of a seventy-billion-parameter model on an H one hundred. You can count the mismatch in time, or in work per byte.
In time, reading a hundred and forty gigabytes of weights at three point three five terabytes a second takes forty-one point eight milliseconds.
The arithmetic, a hundred and forty billion operations at nine hundred and eighty-nine trillion a second, takes zero point one four one milliseconds.
Divide forty-one point eight by zero point one four one, and you get two hundred and ninety-five. The arithmetic units are busy zero point three four percent of the time.
In work, decode does one operation for every byte it reads, but the chip can do two hundred and ninety-five operations in the time one byte arrives.
This gap is not just about time. On a chip bounded by heat and power, moving data is also where the energy goes.
Adding two thirty-two-bit floating-point numbers costs about zero point nine picojoules. Multiplying them costs three point seven.
Reading that same number from a fast on-chip cache costs five picojoules, roughly in line with the arithmetic.
Fetching that number from D RAM beside the chip costs six hundred and forty picojoules: more than seven hundred times the energy of adding it.
A G P U is built around one single bet about the workload: it is the same few operations, repeated across billions of numbers.
In sequence, one worker finishes four jobs in four units of time. In parallel, four workers finish all four jobs in one unit.
Parallelism only works when jobs do not depend on one another. If job two needs the output of job one, it cannot start early.
A transformer generates tokens one at a time, but inside each token sits a matrix multiply of sixteen million independent operations.
Everything in this processor follows from answering three questions.
First: why is this chip designed so differently from a laptop C P U? Because it trades clever prediction for thousands of parallel lanes.
Second: why is moving a byte so expensive next to computing an operation? Because of the physics of memory cells and the ladder of caches.
And third: what can the hardware do to fight back? By hiding latency behind warps, packing bytes into sectors, and reusing data in tensor cores.
A general-purpose C P U core never knows what instruction is coming next. It could be arithmetic, a jump, or a decision based on data not yet computed.
So it spends most of its silicon on anticipation: predicting which way branches will go, reordering instructions, and prefetching data before anyone asks.
When code reaches a branch, the C P U guesses the outcome and runs ahead. Guess right, and the work was free. Guess wrong, and everything computed is thrown away.
All that machinery pays off when a single thread makes unpredictable turns. But on a matrix multiply, where every instruction is predictable, it is pure overhead.
The G P U makes the opposite trade. It strips away branch predictors and speculative execution, and fills the silicon with arithmetic lanes.
One multiprocessor holds up to two thousand and forty-eight threads. None of them is fast on its own, and none of them gets anticipation machinery.
The G P U does not try to avoid waiting. It simply arranges to always have another warp ready to run.
And that single design is stamped one hundred and thirty-two times across the die: over two hundred and seventy thousand threads in flight at once.
To follow the hardware specifications, we must keep three kinds of names apart: the architecture, the chip, and the system.
An architecture is the blueprint: Volta in twenty-seventeen, Ampere in twenty-twenty, Hopper in twenty-twenty-two, and Blackwell in twenty-twenty-four.
A chip is one physical product built to that design: the H one hundred has one hundred and thirty-two multiprocessors, and the H two hundred adds faster memory.
Systems are what get wired together: a D G X box joins eight G P Us with N V Link, while an N V L seventy-two rack joins seventy-two G P Us into one single domain.
When a workload is the same arithmetic over a billion numbers, one hundred thousand slow lanes in parallel beat a handful of fast cores by orders of magnitude.
Where does this bet lose? On work that forms a serial chain, where every step needs the answer from the step before.
A chain runs at the speed of one lane, and one G P U lane is far slower than a C P U core.
Generating tokens is a chain between tokens, but inside each token sits a matrix multiply millions of numbers wide. The lanes have plenty of parallel work.
Open up one multiprocessor, and you find two completely different kinds of maths units.
First, one hundred and twenty-eight C U D A cores. Each one is a scalar unit that performs one multiply-add every cycle.
Second, four tensor cores. These do not operate on single numbers; they calculate on whole matrix tiles at once.
Every other piece of silicon on the multiprocessor exists for one reason: to keep these two sets of units fed with data.
The headline number on the specification sheet comes almost entirely from the four tensor cores, not the one hundred and twenty-eight scalar cores.
At thirty-two bits, all sixteen thousand scalar cores across the chip deliver sixty-six point nine trillion operations a second.
At sixteen bits, pairing numbers together, they reach one hundred and thirty-three point eight trillion.
At that same sixteen-bit precision, the five hundred and twenty-eight tensor cores deliver nine hundred and eighty-nine point four trillion: over seven times ahead.
You can derive that headline number yourself by multiplying out four hardware factors.
One hundred and thirty-two multiprocessors times four tensor cores gives five hundred and twenty-eight tensor cores across the chip.
Each tensor core completes five hundred and twelve multiply-adds every single tick. That is one thousand and twenty-four operations per tick.
Multiply by one point eight three billion ticks a second, and you land on nine hundred and eighty-nine point four trillion operations every second.
An arithmetic unit cannot reach into memory. It can only read from a register and write to a register.
The register step is not optional. Every number must land in a register before the maths can touch it.
Each multiprocessor contains two hundred and fifty-six kilobytes of registers, giving sixty-five thousand five hundred and thirty-six slots.
Those registers are partitioned across resident threads. Give each thread thirty-two registers, and all two thousand and forty-eight threads fit.
Double the registers to sixty-four, and only half as many threads fit. Hoarding registers buys speed per thread, but leaves fewer threads to hide memory waits.
Beside the registers sits another two hundred and fifty-six kilobytes of fast S RAM.
The programmer can claim up to two hundred and twenty-eight kilobytes of this as shared memory, a scratchpad managed by software.
Whatever is not claimed serves as an automatic L one cache.
Shared memory exists to enable tiling: staging data so cooperating threads can share it without hitting memory.
Each output cell needs four numbers from row A and four numbers from column B, eight numbers in all.
If all sixteen threads fetched their own eight numbers from memory, the block would make a hundred and twenty-eight reads.
Instead, the block copies the sixteen numbers of A and sixteen of B into shared memory once, making thirty-two reads in all.
Every thread then reads from shared memory. That is four times fewer reads, exactly the width of the tile. A tile a hundred and twenty-eight wide saves a hundred and twenty-eight times.
A cache is simply a small, fast copy of something slow and far away. It works only when programs reuse data.
A program that touches every number exactly once gains nothing from any cache, however large. Generating one token touches every weight once.
Both cache and shared memory use the same physical silicon. The difference is who decides what is in them.
When streaming through weights, guessing is useless. Stating exactly which tiles to stage is everything.

chapter.title: Schedulers, the copy engine, four quarters
chapter.kicker: 07 · Schedulers, the copy engine, four quarters

beats.text: Every multiprocessor contains four independent hardware schedulers.
The sixty-four groups of threads resident on the multiprocessor are divided equally: each scheduler owns sixteen of them.
Every single cycle, each scheduler looks across its sixteen groups: whose data has arrived? Who is ready to calculate?
In hardware, in a single tick, it picks one ready group and issues its next instruction across thirty-two lanes.
If none of its sixteen groups is ready, that scheduler's lanes sit idle for the cycle. That is the exact failure this chip is built to avoid.

chapter.title: Schedulers, the copy engine, four quarters
chapter.kicker: 07 · Schedulers, the copy engine, four quarters

beats.text: On older chips, threads had to spend their own arithmetic instructions copying data from memory into shared scratchpads.
For a sixty-four by sixty-four tile, that meant one hundred and twenty-eight threads issuing five hundred and twelve copy instructions: five hundred slots not spent on maths.
Hopper adds the T M A, the tensor memory accelerator: a dedicated hardware copy engine that runs independently of the execution lanes.
The programmer gives it a descriptor: the start address, the shape of the tile, and the row stride. One single thread issues one single instruction.
The engine works out all sixty-four row addresses itself and streams the tile straight into shared memory in the background, while the threads carry on computing.

chapter.title: Schedulers, the copy engine, four quarters
chapter.kicker: 07 · Schedulers, the copy engine, four quarters

beats.text: Now we can see how the entire multiprocessor fits together: it is four identical quarters.
Each quarter owns its own scheduler, thirty-two scalar lanes, one tensor core, and sixteen thousand three hundred and eighty-four registers.
The two hundred and fifty-six kilobytes of shared memory and the T M A copy engine sit at the center, shared by all four quarters.
Notice the arithmetic: one hundred and twenty-eight lanes divided by four schedulers is exactly thirty-two lanes per scheduler.
That thirty-two is the atomic group size of the machine. The warp.

chapter.title: Schedulers, the copy engine, four quarters
chapter.kicker: 07 · Schedulers, the copy engine, four quarters

beats.text: Thirty-two threads make a warp. Threads on a G P U never move one at a time; they always move in warps of thirty-two.
This model is called S I M T: single instruction, multiple threads.
The instruction is fetched once, decoded once, and fired across all thirty-two lanes in lockstep.
Every lane runs the exact same addition, but each lane points at its own data in its own registers.
A kernel is the program the G P U runs. It is written once, for a single thread, and launched across millions of threads.
Every thread runs those identical lines. The only thing that differs is its number.
Thread five of block three works out its index: three times two hundred and fifty-six plus five gives seven hundred and seventy-three.
Neighbouring threads get neighbouring indices. A warp of thirty-two threads reads thirty-two numbers lying side by side in memory: one hundred and twenty-eight consecutive bytes.
When software launches a kernel, it requests a grid of blocks.
A block holds up to one thousand and twenty-four threads, which is thirty-two warps. The hardware places each block whole on one multiprocessor.
A multiprocessor holds up to two thousand and forty-eight threads: two full blocks of one thousand and twenty-four, or eight blocks of two hundred and fifty-six.
Shared memory belongs to a block. All its threads share the same scratchpad, which is why a block is the unit that cooperates.
Thirty-two lanes moving in lockstep sounds rigid. Why not let every thread execute independently?
Because independent execution requires thirty-two independent instruction decoders, branch trackers, and instruction caches.
An instruction is itself a number, a hundred and twenty-eight bits of data stored in memory. Fetching and decoding it costs real energy and real silicon.
A scalar C P U core pays that decode cost for every single operation. A G P U warp pays it once and spreads it across thirty-two lanes.
Sixty-four warps of thirty-two threads fill one multiprocessor to capacity: two thousand and forty-eight resident threads.
Every cycle, each of the four schedulers issues one instruction. Spread over sixteen warps, each thread moves once every sixteen ticks.
At nearly two billion ticks a second, that is about a hundred and twenty-four million instructions a second per thread.
Across the entire chip, that adds up to thirty-three point five trillion thread-instructions every second. The speed is in the count, not in any single thread.
To keep any delivery pipeline full, you must know how much work has to be on the road.
If a pizza leaves every five minutes and a round trip takes thirty minutes, you need six drivers on the road at all times, or the oven sits idle.

This is Little's law. For high-bandwidth memory delivering three thousand three hundred and fifty-two bytes a nanosecond across a two hundred and seventy nanosecond trip, nine hundred and fifteen thousand bytes must be on the road at every moment.
Divided across one hundred and thirty-two multiprocessors, each unit must keep about seven thousand bytes in flight.
If every one of the two thousand and forty-eight threads has one four-byte load outstanding, that is eight thousand bytes: just enough to saturate the bus.
Here is the complete hierarchy of execution on the chip, from the thread to the package.
Thirty-two threads make a warp, executing one shared instruction in lockstep.
A block holds up to thirty-two warps, sharing one slice of on-chip scratchpad memory.
A multiprocessor holds up to sixty-four warps across four schedulers, and one hundred and thirty-two multiprocessors make the chip.
On an ordinary processor, a conditional branch is routine. One thread reaches a decision, takes one path, and carries on.
On a G P U, thirty-two lanes reach that fork together sharing one instruction, but the numbers they are testing differ in every lane.
There is only one instruction decoder, so the hardware cannot run both branches at once. It runs them back to back, masking off half the lanes in each pass.
Each lane sits completely idle through the half it skipped. A balanced if-else branch cuts throughput in half.
The hardware enforces divergence using an active bitmask: one bit for each of the thirty-two lanes.
Inactive lanes still occupy their place in the execution slot. They simply discard the result.
Each nested fork doubles the passes: one fork means two passes; two nested forks mean four passes; three nested forks mean eight passes.
A branch costs nothing when all thirty-two lanes take the same path. Divergence only happens when lanes disagree.
Divergence is the first of two cardinal sins in G P U programming. The second is uncoalesced memory access.
Both sins have the exact same cause: thirty-two lanes that are bound together by hardware to act as one.
Divergence happens when lanes want different instructions, wasting arithmetic issue slots.
Uncoalesced access happens when lanes want scattered memory addresses, wasting memory bandwidth. And bandwidth is by far the scarcer resource.

chapter.title: Why memory is slow in the first place
chapter.kicker: 11 · Why memory is slow in the first place

beats.text: The memory hierarchy is not an arbitrary design choice. It follows directly from the physics of a memory cell.
An S RAM cell uses six transistors to form two loops that actively reinforce each other. It can be read in a single cycle without disturbing its state.
A D RAM cell uses just one transistor and one tiny capacitor. The bit is stored as a microscopic packet of electrical charge.
Because it uses one transistor instead of six, D RAM is far denser and cheaper per bit: that is how eighty gigabytes fits beside the chip. But a capacitor leaks like a bucket with a hole.

chapter.title: Why memory is slow in the first place
chapter.kicker: 11 · Why memory is slow in the first place

beats.text: Reading a D RAM cell destroys the bit. The stored charge is so small that measuring it drains it completely.
Every read is therefore a read followed by an immediate rewrite, and that memory row is blocked until the rewrite finishes.
Because the charge leaks away continuously, the memory controller must also rewrite every row on a timer: every sixty-four milliseconds.
These physical constraints make D RAM slower to respond. But they do not limit bandwidth: bandwidth comes from wires.

chapter.title: Why memory is slow in the first place
chapter.kicker: 11 · Why memory is slow in the first place

beats.text: When a thread requests a number from high-bandwidth memory, the journey takes about two hundred and seventy-three nanoseconds.
The memory cell itself takes only twenty-seven point five nanoseconds to open a row and read a column: barely a tenth of the total time.
Most of the wait is the journey: checking local caches, crossing the chip to the memory controller, waiting in queues, and traveling across package traces.
Wider buses do not shorten that journey. More wires carry more bytes at once, but they do not make signals travel faster across silicon.

chapter.title: Why memory is slow in the first place
chapter.kicker: 11 · Why memory is slow in the first place

beats.text: In every computer ever built, storage technologies face the exact same trade: speed against capacity.
The top-right corner is completely empty. No technology exists that is both the fastest and the largest.
Speed requires physical proximity: to be fast, a memory must be microscopic and sit right next to the arithmetic.
Large capacity requires surface area, which inevitably pushes memory further away across longer wires. The only possible solution is a ladder.

chapter.title: Why memory is slow in the first place
chapter.kicker: 11 · Why memory is slow in the first place

beats.text: The hardware organizes memory into four rungs: registers, L one and shared memory, the L two cache, and H B M.
Counted across the whole chip, the registers hold thirty-four point six megabytes, while H B M holds eighty gigabytes: about twenty-five hundred times as much.
Each rung is also defined by scope: who is allowed to see it. Registers belong to a single thread and nobody else.
Shared memory is seen by all threads in one block. The L two cache is seen by all multiprocessors. H B M is seen by everything, including other chips.
Sum up every single byte of fast storage on the chip: all the registers, all the shared memory, and the entire L two cache.
Together, they hold one hundred and twenty-one point six megabytes. A seventy-billion-parameter model takes a hundred and forty gigabytes.
All the fast memory on the chip holds less than a thousandth of the model: zero point zero eight seven percent.
Generating a token reads every weight once, so by the time a weight could be reused, thousands of others have evicted it. Every token's weights must come up from H B M.
Measured on real hardware, latency climbs steeply with every step down the ladder.
Bandwidth falls just as fast in the other direction.
Top to bottom, latency grows nearly five hundred times, while bandwidth drops a hundred and twenty times.
Reaching down to H B M for a byte is vastly more expensive than computing on a byte already at the top. G P U programming is the craft of staging data upward.

chapter.title: How the chip survives slow memory
chapter.kicker: 13 · How the chip survives slow memory

beats.text: A cook preparing dinner does not stand in front of the oven watching it bake. While one dish cooks, the cook chops vegetables for the next.
The oven takes the exact same time either way. Nothing was made faster. The wait was covered with other work. That is latency hiding.
When warp zero asks for a number from memory, it stalls for nearly five hundred clock cycles.
Instead of waiting, the scheduler immediately runs warp one, then warp two, then warp three. By the time warp zero's data arrives, dozens of other warps have computed.

chapter.title: How the chip survives slow memory
chapter.kicker: 13 · How the chip survives slow memory

beats.text: On an ordinary processor, switching between threads is expensive. The C P U must save one thread's registers to memory and reload another's.
On this chip, switching between resident warps costs zero cycles. Nothing is saved and nothing is restored.
Because the register file holds sixty-five thousand registers, every resident thread already owns its private slice of physical storage.
The hardware simply points its issue logic at a different warp next cycle. The chip pays in silicon area, once, instead of in cycles, constantly.

chapter.title: How the chip survives slow memory
chapter.kicker: 13 · How the chip survives slow memory

beats.text: How many warps does a scheduler need to hide a five-hundred-tick memory load? It depends on how much work each warp does between loads.
If a warp computes thirty-two instructions between memory loads, the scheduler needs exactly sixteen warps: all sixteen it can hold.
If a warp computes only eight instructions between loads, it would need sixty-one warps. Even full occupancy leaves the scheduler idle three quarters of the time.
Occupancy cannot hide latency when there is too little arithmetic between loads: the ratio of compute to memory sets the pace.

chapter.title: How the chip survives slow memory
chapter.kicker: 13 · How the chip survives slow memory

beats.text: Four separate hardware limits govern how many warps can reside on a multiprocessor for any given kernel.
A thread using more registers leaves room for fewer threads. A block claiming more shared memory leaves room for fewer blocks.
Blocks are placed whole, so whichever resource runs out first sets the occupancy.
Remember that occupancy is a latency-hiding metric, not a speed metric. A well-tuned kernel at fifty percent occupancy often beats a careless one at one hundred percent.

chapter.title: How the chip survives slow memory
chapter.kicker: 13 · How the chip survives slow memory

beats.text: The memory system never hands over a single number. It moves data in thirty-two-byte sectors, four to a hundred-and-twenty-eight-byte line.
A sector comes whole even if a thread only asked for one number in it.
Here is the perfect match: thirty-two threads in a warp, reading thirty-two neighbouring four-byte numbers, need exactly one hundred and twenty-eight bytes: one line, four sectors, every byte wanted.
Scatter those thirty-two lanes into different sectors, and thirty-two sectors come up across the bus: over a thousand bytes moved to use one hundred and twenty-eight. Eight times the memory traffic.
In physical memory, a two-dimensional grid of numbers is stored as one long continuous line, row after row.
Neighbours along a row sit right next to each other, four bytes apart. But neighbours down a column sit thousands of bytes apart.
In a matrix four thousand numbers wide, one step down a column is sixteen thousand bytes. A warp walking a column puts every single lane in a separate sector.
Walking a row is cheap; walking a column costs eight times the memory traffic, without changing a single mathematical operation.
Stride is the distance in memory between numbers requested by neighbouring threads.
At stride one, the warp reads adjacent numbers: four sectors carry everything, and useful efficiency is one hundred percent.
Double the stride to two, and it touches eight sectors: fifty percent efficiency. Double to four, and it touches sixteen: twenty-five percent.
At a stride of eight four-byte numbers, thirty-two bytes, every lane has a sector to itself. One thousand and twenty-four bytes are moved to use one hundred and twenty-eight.
Beyond that, the waste cannot get worse; the lanes simply spread across more cache lines. This is why kernel optimisation is largely the art of making every fetched byte count.
Roughly every two years, a new G P U architecture arrives on a smaller manufacturing process.

Over seven years, dense sixteen-bit arithmetic grew eighteen-fold: from a hundred and twenty-five trillion operations on the V one hundred to twenty-two hundred and fifty trillion on the B two hundred.
Over that same period, memory bandwidth grew only nine-fold: from zero point nine terabytes a second to eight terabytes.

The ridge, the ratio between them, doubled from a hundred and thirty-nine to nearly three hundred. Work that kept a V one hundred fully busy can sit memory-bound on an H one hundred without changing a single line of code.
Why could the two curves never keep pace? Because adding arithmetic requires area, and transistors have been shrinking for fifty years.
Bandwidth requires physical wires, and wires take real space.
You can run a thousand parallel signals over millimetres on a package. You can run dozens over centimetres across a board. You can run four down a cable across a room.
One curve is limited by how small a transistor can be printed. The other is limited by how many wires will fit between two objects. They were never going to grow at the same rate.
At sixteen bits, the ridge doubled and leveled off. But look at each chip's narrowest number format, and the climb is dramatic.
Every new generation introduces a narrower number: eight-bit floats on Hopper, four-bit floats on Blackwell.
Halving the bits doubles operations per second on the same silicon, while memory bandwidth gets no such multiplier.
At each chip's narrowest format, the ridge shoots from a hundred and thirty-nine on the V one hundred to over eleven hundred on the B two hundred: an eightfold climb.
NVIDIA ran the controlled experiment themselves with the H two hundred.

The compute die is completely identical: the same multiprocessors, the same peak operations per second. The only thing that changed is memory: four point eight terabytes a second, forty-three percent faster.
For a seventy-billion-parameter model at eight bits, the token rate jumps from forty-seven point nine to sixty-eight point six tokens a second: the exact same forty-three percent gain.
Every generation attacks the wall the same three ways: lower precision to shrink the bytes, faster memory to move more bytes, and wider links between chips.
Attainable performance is the absolute ceiling this chip could reach on a given algorithm. It is not a prediction; it is an upper bound.
Below the ridge, the slanted roof binds: the chip can do no more operations per second than memory bandwidth times arithmetic intensity.
Above the ridge, the flat ceiling binds: the tensor cores' peak of nine hundred and eighty-nine trillion operations a second.
The inflection point where they meet is the ridge: nine hundred and eighty-nine trillion divided by three point three five trillion bytes, giving two hundred and ninety-five operations per byte.
Now place the two phases of running a language model onto that roofline.
Decode generates one token at a time, multiplying the token's vector by the weights. Each weight is read once, giving one operation per byte.
Prefill processes a whole prompt of thousands of tokens at once, reusing each weight thousands of times: one to two thousand operations per byte.
The exact same model on the exact same hardware lives on opposite sides of the ridge: decode is starved for memory; prefill saturates the maths units.
Look at two basic mathematical operations to see how arithmetic intensity is set.
Adding two arrays reads two numbers and writes one: six bytes of traffic for one addition, or zero point one seven operations per byte.
Multiplying two thousand-by-thousand matrices performs over two billion operations on six megabytes of data: three hundred and forty-one operations per byte.
They sit two thousand times apart, and neither number depends on the G P U. The chip sets the ridge; mathematics decides which side you land on.
To multiply two matrices, every row of the first meets every column of the second.
Multiply the pairs, add the products, and you get one entry of the result: one times five plus two times seven equals nineteen.
For two matrices of size n, calculating the output takes n cubed operations from two n squared numbers. Every single number is reused n times.
When matrix B has only one column, each weight is used once: that is decode. When B has many columns of tokens, every weight is reused: that is prefill.
A scalar C U D A core multiplies two numbers and adds a third, producing one number per cycle.
A tensor core multiplies two small matrices and adds a third, producing a whole tile of outputs at once.
Inside Hopper, a single tensor core finishes five hundred and twelve multiply-adds every single tick: over a thousand operations per cycle.
One single warp instruction executes a sixteen by eight by sixteen step: two thousand and forty-eight multiply-adds, keeping one core busy for four ticks.
Bigger tiles feed themselves: the larger the tile, the more times each fetched number is reused.
A two-by-two tile reuses each number twice, delivering one operation per byte.
A sixteen-by-sixteen tile reuses each number sixteen times: eight operations per byte. A tile a hundred and twenty-eight wide reuses each number a hundred and twenty-eight times.
That is why tensor cores operate on tiles, why kernels stage large tiles in scratchpad memory, and why prefill saturates the hardware while decode cannot.
Why dedicate five hundred and twenty-eight specialized units to a single mathematical operation?
Because modern transformers spend well over ninety percent of their arithmetic on matrix multiplication.
Peak performance assumes every single unit is fed with data every single cycle without a stall. Real code never reaches it.
A superbly tuned kernel reaches fifty to eighty percent of peak. Compare chips on their peak; compare software on how close to peak it gets.
Lower precision is the single lever that attacks both bottlenecks at the exact same time.
On the arithmetic side, narrower numbers allow tensor cores to process twice as many calculations each second.
On the memory side, narrower numbers mean fewer bytes cross the bus for every weight. You move less data to do the same work.
Multiplying in binary is simply long multiplication with a trivial times table: each digit is either zero or one.
Multiply eleven by thirteen, and the shifted rows sum to one hundred and forty-three.
Every bit of the first number pairs with every bit of the second through an A N D gate. The work grows with the square of the width.

Sixteen gates at four bits, sixty-four at eight bits, two hundred and fifty-six at sixteen bits, and over a thousand at thirty-two bits. Halve the bit width, and the multiplier circuit shrinks to a quarter.
By silicon area alone, the footprint of one thirty-two-bit multiplier can fit sixteen eight-bit multipliers.
Yet when an H one hundred switches from sixteen-bit to eight-bit numbers, its throughput doubles rather than quadrupling: from nine hundred and eighty-nine trillion to nearly two thousand trillion.
Why twice and not four times? Because of operand delivery. The internal wires carrying numbers to the units have a fixed bit width.
The square law sets how much arithmetic fits in silicon. Data delivery sets how fast it can be fed.
Every tensor-core generation has introduced a narrower native format.
Volta introduced sixteen-bit tensor cores in twenty-seventeen at a hundred and twenty-five trillion operations a second.
Hopper introduced eight-bit floats at nearly two thousand trillion. Blackwell introduces four-bit floats at nine thousand trillion operations a second.
From Volta's sixteen-bit rate to Blackwell's four-bit rate is a seventy-two-fold increase in dense arithmetic throughput.
Scientific notation writes a number as a few digits multiplied by a power of ten, where the power dictates where the decimal point lands.
A floating-point number does the exact same thing in base two. Six is one one zero in binary, which is one point one times two squared.

In standard thirty-two-bit floating point, the sign bit is zero for positive. The exponent field holds the power plus a bias of one hundred and twenty-seven, so two squared is stored as one hundred and twenty-nine.

The fraction field holds the bits after the binary point. Because the bit before the point is always one, the hardware never stores it, gaining twenty-four significant bits of precision from twenty-three bits of storage.
Range and precision are bought separately, and with a fixed budget of bits, every bit given to one is stolen from the other.
More exponent bits allow a format to reach vastly larger and smaller magnitudes. More fraction bits allow it to distinguish tiny differences between nearby numbers.
Standard sixteen-bit floating point keeps ten fraction bits and five exponent bits, giving fine steps over a narrow range.

B float sixteen does the exact opposite. It preserves all eight exponent bits from thirty-two-bit float, keeping its immense range while trimming the fraction to seven bits. It is simply the top half of a thirty-two-bit number.
Read field by field, pi in B float sixteen reveals the mechanics with complete clarity.
The sign bit is zero, positive. The exponent is one zero zero zero zero zero zero zero, which is one hundred and twenty-eight. Subtracting the bias leaves one, so the power is two to the first power.
The seven fraction bits spell out seventy-three over one hundred and twenty-eight. Adding the implicit leading one gives one point five seven zero three one two five.

Multiply by two, and the value is exactly three point one four zero six two five. Pi is three point one four one five nine, so B float sixteen is off by less than one thousandth, an error of barely zero point zero three percent.
Look at the reach: standard sixteen-bit float maxes out at sixty-five thousand five hundred and four, while B float sixteen reaches ten to the thirty-eighth power.
B float sixteen reaches five times ten to the thirty-third power higher, completely banishing the numerical overflow that plagued early neural network training.
The price is precision: just above one, sixteen-bit float places numbers every zero point zero zero zero nine eight, while B float sixteen steps eight times coarser.
That is the whole bargain: deep learning forgives coarse rounding on individual weights, but requires enormous dynamic range across layers.
When multiplying two floating-point numbers, the exponents add, and the significands multiply.
Because an eight-by-eight multiplier takes sixty-four gates versus five hundred and seventy-six for twenty-four bits, a B float sixteen multiplier is a ninth the size of a thirty-two-bit unit.
Yet on an H one hundred, B float sixteen runs at the exact same rate as sixteen-bit float, nine hundred and eighty-nine trillion operations a second, even though its multiplier is half the size.
Silicon area determines how many multipliers can fit on a die. But operand delivery wires determine how fast they can be fed numbers each tick.
To preserve accuracy across millions of multiply-adds, modern hardware employs a crucial safeguard: low-precision multiplies accumulate into a thirty-two-bit floating-point total.
If you add one repeatedly in pure B float sixteen, the running total stops advancing completely at two hundred and fifty-six.

Above two hundred and fifty-six, the gap between consecutive B float numbers widens to two. Adding one lands on a midpoint that rounds right back down to two hundred and fifty-six, vanishing into thin air.

Standard sixteen-bit float hits the same wall at two thousand and forty-eight. Accumulating in thirty-two-bit float counts past sixteen million with zero rounding loss, protecting dot products across deep layers.
When marketing announcements boast of nine-fold or eighteen-fold leaps between chip generations, look closely at what is being measured.
Those headline multiples almost always blend reduced precision, structural sparsity, and clustered network fabrics together into a single theoretical number.
On identical precision and dense workloads, real silicon progress typically delivers a solid two to four times improvement per generation.
Understanding the three physical attacks on the memory wall lets you separate true architectural advances from marketing arithmetic.

chapter.title: When one chip is not enough
chapter.kicker: 20 · When one chip is not enough

beats.text: Even if memory bandwidth were infinite, frontier models hit a hard wall before running a single calculation: capacity.
An H one hundred holds eighty gigabytes, and an H two hundred holds one hundred and forty-one gigabytes. No amount of bandwidth helps if the model cannot physically fit.
At sixteen bits, Llama three four hundred and five billion takes eight hundred and ten gigabytes of weights alone, requiring eleven H one hundreds before allocating a single byte for working memory.
A standard chassis of eight H one hundreds holds six hundred and forty gigabytes. At sixteen bits, the weights spill into a second chassis, forcing communication out onto the cluster network.

chapter.title: When one chip is not enough
chapter.kicker: 20 · When one chip is not enough

beats.text: When a model is split across chips, they must communicate continuously. What joins them is an interconnect link.
An interconnect link is simply a bundle of wires between chips, governed by the exact same width times frequency arithmetic as any internal bus.
The only difference is distance. Fewer wires stretching across longer physical space mean slower speeds and higher energy per bit.
A chip has three distinct bandwidths: to its own memory, to a neighbouring chip, and out to the network. Each is several times slower than the last.

chapter.title: When one chip is not enough
chapter.kicker: 20 · When one chip is not enough

beats.text: Clustering divides cleanly into two domains: scale up and scale out.
Scale up connects graphics processors inside a single enclosure using high-speed proprietary links and crossbar switches.
Scale out connects separate chassis across the room through conventional data-centre network cables.
The boundary between the two is the most critical line in a data centre: whatever data crosses that boundary pays a nine-fold penalty in speed.

chapter.title: When one chip is not enough
chapter.kicker: 20 · When one chip is not enough

beats.text: Wiring every pair of graphics processors directly together quickly becomes impossible as clusters grow.
Connecting every pair of n chips requires n times n minus one divided by two links: six links for four chips, twenty-eight for eight, and over two thousand five hundred for seventy-two chips.
Because an H one hundred has a fixed budget of eighteen links, direct wiring splits each chip's bandwidth seven ways, leaving most links idle during point-to-point transfers.
A crossbar switch solves this completely. Every chip runs all its links straight to the switch, enabling any pair to communicate at maximum speed while connections scale linearly.

chapter.title: When one chip is not enough
chapter.kicker: 20 · When one chip is not enough

beats.text: Interconnect bandwidth has grown rapidly across generations, yet the ratio to local memory remains stubbornly fixed.
On the A one hundred, local memory ran at two terabytes per second while neighbouring links provided three hundred gigabytes per second each way, a gap of nearly seven times.
On the H one hundred, memory grew to over three point three terabytes while links rose to four hundred and fifty gigabytes each way, maintaining a seven-point-four-fold gap.
Blackwell reaches eight terabytes per second of memory and nine hundred gigabytes of link bandwidth each way. Local memory is always roughly eight times faster than reaching across the board.

chapter.title: When one chip is not enough
chapter.kicker: 20 · When one chip is not enough

beats.text: Why is leaving the package so punishing? The answer is pure geometry.
Inside the package, silicon interposers pack five thousand one hundred and twenty microscopic wires running over mere millimetres, delivering three point three five terabytes per second.
Off the package, circuit boards accommodate only seventy-two wire pairs over centimetres, dropping bandwidth to four hundred and fifty gigabytes per second each way, over seven times slower.

Across the room, an InfiniBand cable provides fifty gigabytes per second each way, nine times slower again. Driving longer distances demands vastly more power, forcing fewer wires and lower throughput.

chapter.title: When one chip is not enough
chapter.kicker: 20 · When one chip is not enough

beats.text: Tensor parallelism splits the weight matrices of each layer across multiple graphics processors.
To compute an output dot product, each chip multiplies its half of the inputs and weights, producing a partial sum.
Before the next layer can begin, the chips must exchange their partial sums in an operation called an all-reduce, so both arrive at the complete answer of eighteen.

Modern architectures perform two all-reduces per layer. In an eighty-layer model, that means one hundred and sixty synchronization barriers for every single token generated. Inside a switch fabric that exchange is viable; across a network cable it is catastrophic.

chapter.title: When one chip is not enough
chapter.kicker: 20 · When one chip is not enough

beats.text: Because crossing between scale up and scale out is so punishing, the primary hardware strategy is to make the fast domain as large as possible.
For years, the standard domain size was fixed at eight graphics processors in a single server chassis.
The liquid-cooled rack unites seventy-two graphics processors into a single seamless switch domain, containing over thirteen terabytes of memory.
Any chip in the entire rack can reach any other at full link bandwidth, keeping even massive frontier models inside the fast neighbourhood and off the external network.

chapter.title: Other bets, and the three answers
chapter.kicker: 21 · Other bets, and the three answers

beats.text: The graphics multiprocessor is one way to organise silicon around matrix multiplication, but it is not the only way.
Google's tensor processing unit makes a radically different bet: a massive, rigid two-dimensional grid of multiply-accumulate cells called a systolic array.
Data streams in from the edges, and each cell passes its intermediate product directly to its neighbour on every clock tick, with zero round trips back to a register file.
Where a graphics processor solves arithmetic intensity through software caching and thread scheduling, a systolic array bakes data reuse directly into the copper wiring.

chapter.title: Other bets, and the three answers
chapter.kicker: 21 · Other bets, and the three answers

beats.text: Watch a three-by-three systolic array step through time. Weights are held stationary inside each cell, while input values enter on a slant from the left.
On each beat, a cell multiplies its stored weight by the number arriving from the left, adds the sum arriving from above, and passes both forward.
In just seven beats, all twenty-seven multiply-adds finish, and completed results emerge from the bottom of each column without a single trip to memory.
Production units expand this to one hundred and twenty-eight cells on a side, executing sixteen thousand three hundred and eighty-four operations on every single clock beat.

chapter.title: Other bets, and the three answers
chapter.kicker: 21 · Other bets, and the three answers

beats.text: On pure hardware specifications, competition is fierce. AMD's M I three hundred X offers one hundred and ninety-two gigabytes of fast memory against eighty on an H one hundred, letting models that require two chips fit onto one.
Yet most artificial intelligence teams continue to choose Nvidia. The deciding factor is not silicon physics, but software.
Between a model and bare silicon sit four distinct layers: high-level frameworks, thousands of hand-tuned math libraries, optimizing compilers, and hardware drivers.
CUDA has had twenty years to accumulate finely tuned kernels for every conceivable operation. A chip specification describes only the silicon layer at the bottom, but teams experience all four.

chapter.title: Other bets, and the three answers
chapter.kicker: 21 · Other bets, and the three answers

beats.text: We can now answer the three fundamental questions we began with.

Why is this chip so different from a laptop C P U? Because it makes one foundational bet: modern work consists of billions of identical operations. It discards complex branch anticipation to pack sixteen thousand arithmetic lanes and five hundred tensor cores onto a single die.

Why is a byte so expensive next to an operation? Because of physics. A memory cell is a tiny capacitor hidden behind millimetres of wire, creating a two-hundred-and-ninety-five to one gap between arithmetic and data delivery.

And what does the hardware do to fight back? It hides latency behind thousands of resident threads, coalesces bytes into clean thirty-two-byte sectors, reuses numbers dozens of times inside tensor cores, halves precision to shrink circuits, and unifies entire racks into single high-speed domains.
Hardware provides the raw silicon capability. But how code unlocks that capability, and how software commands these multiprocessors, is the subject of the next film: inside G P U kernels.
